boundary_rationale: The book opens with the verse-initial formula וַיְהִ֖י בִּימֵ֣י אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ “Now in the days of Ahasuerus” web:Esth.1.1, an opening formula occurring nowhere else in the book (sweep: 1 book-wide as a verse-initial opener), paired with the merism מֵהֹ֣דּוּ וְעַד כּ֔וּשׁ “from India even to Ethiopia” web:Esth.1.1 that sets the empire’s scope (sweep: 2 book-wide; the same merism recurs once more, at 8:9, framing the edict and its counter-edict). After the throne-and-Susa setting in 1:2, a fresh regnal-year clause בִּשְׁנַ֤ת שָׁלוֹשׁ֙ לְמָלְכ֔וֹ “in the third year of his reign” web:Esth.1.3 launches the nobles’ banquet, which the unit closes out with its own duration notice יָמִ֣ים רַבִּ֔ים שְׁמוֹנִ֥ים וּמְאַ֖ת יֽוֹם “many days, even one hundred eighty days” web:Esth.1.4, before a second transition formula opens the next unit at 1:5.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 1:1-2 as a self-contained unit would strand the royal formula from the very banquet it exists to introduce.

boundary_rationale: A new temporal-transition clause וּבִמְל֣וֹאת הַיָּמִ֣ים הָאֵ֗לֶּה “When these days were fulfilled” web:Esth.1.5 marks a distinct banquet from the one just closed, this one for all the people of Susa, carrying its own wine-protocol note through 1:8. The particle in גַּ֚ם וַשְׁתִּ֣י הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה עָשְׂתָ֖ה מִשְׁתֵּ֣ה נָשִׁ֑ים “Also Vashti the queen made a feast for the women” web:Esth.1.9 signals a parallel banquet rather than a subordinate clause and opens no direct-speech frame of its own, so under the banquet-unit default this verse stays inside the span rather than splitting off; the SAMEKH mark follows 1:9 (oshb:Esth.1.9 (setumah, single-witness)), corroborating the close of the unit at exactly this point.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Peeling 1:9 into its own decision would fragment a banquet pairing that no speech frame interrupts.
literature_type_guess: banquet-scene (paired feast and parallel women's feast)

boundary_rationale: A new day-marker בַּיּוֹם֙ הַשְּׁבִיעִ֔י כְּט֥וֹב לֵב הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ בַּיָּ֑יִן “On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine” web:Esth.1.10 opens the crisis: the summons, then the refusal וַתְּמָאֵ֞ן הַמַּלְכָּ֣ה וַשְׁתִּ֗י לָבוֹא֙ “But the queen Vashti refused to come” web:Esth.1.12, closing on the king's wrath in an offline terminal clause, וַחֲמָת֖וֹ בָּעֲרָ֥ה בֽוֹ “and his anger burned in him” web:Esth.1.12; a fresh wayyiqtol then opens 1:13 with a new addressee, וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לַחֲכָמִ֖ים יֹדְעֵ֣י הָֽעִתִּ֑ים “Then the king said to the wise men, who knew the times” web:Esth.1.13, but the king's actual question to them is deferred rather than posed at once: 1:13 goes on to name their standing before all יֹדְעֵ֖י דָּ֥ת וָדִֽין “who knew law and judgment” web:Esth.1.13, and 1:14 lists the seven Persian-and-Median princes, before the quoted question כְּדָת֙ מַֽה לַּעֲשׂ֔וֹת בַּמַּלְכָּ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֑י “What shall we do to Queen Vashti according to law” web:Esth.1.15 finally closes the consultation, before Memucan's answer opens a new speech frame at 1:16. This deferred-question arc — addressee named at 1:13, expertise and personnel specified through 1:14, question posed only at 1:15 — runs as one continuous consultation scene across the 1:12|1:13 clause-type shift rather than splitting there.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting a seam at 1:12|1:13 would divide the deferred-question arc at the point where the addressee is first named but before the king's actual question is posed, three verses later at 1:15.

boundary_rationale: A new speech-formula וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מומכן מְמוּכָ֗ן לִפְנֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְהַשָּׂרִ֔ים “Memucan answered before the king and the princes” web:Esth.1.16 opens Memucan’s direct speech, which runs uninterrupted through the petition-formula recommendation אִם עַל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֗וֹב יֵצֵ֤א דְבַר מַלְכוּת֙ מִלְּפָנָ֔יו “If it pleases the king, let a royal commandment go from him” web:Esth.1.19 (petition formula, sweep: 7 book-wide: 1:19, 3:9, 5:4, 5:8, 7:3, 8:5, 9:13) to the closing rationale about husbands’ honor in 1:20; the return to third-person narration at 1:21 marks the end of the quoted speech and the start of the next unit. Ketiv/qere note: the ketiv מומכן and qere מְמוּכָ֗ן share the same five consonants (mem, mem, vav, kaf, final-nun) with the vav transposed — second position in the ketiv, third in the qere — not a defective/plene difference; disclosed here because 1:16 is quoted.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 1:16-20 into the implementation notice at 1:21-22 would blur the seam between quoted speech and the narration that closes it.

boundary_rationale: Narration resumes with וַיִּיטַב֙ הַדָּבָ֔ר בְּעֵינֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ וְהַשָּׂרִ֑ים “This advice pleased the king and the princes” web:Esth.1.21, a decision-approval formula that closes the quoted-speech unit and opens the implementation, culminating in the dispatch formula וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח סְפָרִים֙ אֶל כָּל מְדִינ֣וֹת הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ “for he sent letters into all the king’s provinces” web:Esth.1.22, each province and people addressed מְדִינָ֤ה וּמְדִינָה֙ כִּכְתָבָ֔הּ וְאֶל עַ֥ם וָעָ֖ם כִּלְשׁוֹנ֑וֹ “every province according to its writing, and to every people in their language” web:Esth.1.22, the same distributive formula core כִּכְתָבָ֔הּ (sweep: 3 verses book-wide: 1:22, 3:12, 8:9) that reappears at the edict (3:12) and the counter-edict (8:9) — not at the edict's own dispatch notice in 3:13, which carries no distributive element at all — together with the doubled distributive מְדִינָ֤ה וּמְדִינָה֙ (sweep: 8 verses book-wide: 1:22, 3:12, 3:14, 4:3, 8:9, 8:13, 8:17, 9:28), also present at both 3:12 and 8:9. The PE mark follows 1:22 (oshb:Esth.1.22 (petuchah, single-witness)), corroborating the chapter-close here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this unit back into Memucan's speech would erase the narration-versus-quoted-speech seam at 1:20|1:21.

boundary_rationale: אַחַר֙ הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה כְּשֹׁ֕ךְ חֲמַ֖ת הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ “After these things, when the wrath of King Ahasuerus was pacified” web:Esth.2.1 opens a new temporal frame with the king’s private reflection on Vashti (byte sweep: 1 book-wide for this exact pointed clause; skeleton sweep: 2 book-wide — 2:1 and 3:1 differ only in accentuation on this opener, and 3:1 alone opens Haman’s rise — an intentional parallel opening both major escalations of the book), which the king’s own servants answer with a proposal-speech וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ נַעֲרֵֽי הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ מְשָׁרְתָ֑יו “Then the king’s servants who served him said” web:Esth.2.2, running through royal approval וַיִּיטַ֧ב הַדָּבָ֛ר בְּעֵינֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ וַיַּ֥עַשׂ כֵּֽן “The thing pleased the king, and he did so” web:Esth.2.4. The SAMEKH mark follows 2:4 (oshb:Esth.2.4 (setumah, single-witness)), closing this unit at the royal-approval formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 2:1 to the end of chapter 1 would ignore the fresh temporal formula that restarts the narrative clock.

boundary_rationale: The character-introduction formula אִ֣ישׁ יְהוּדִ֔י הָיָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֑ה “There was a certain Jew in the citadel of Susa” web:Esth.2.5 (sweep: 1 book-wide, occurring nowhere else) opens named-participant background for Mordecai and, by extension, וַיְהִ֨י אֹמֵ֜ן אֶת הֲדַסָּ֗ה הִ֤יא אֶסְתֵּר֙ “He brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther” web:Esth.2.7, his adopted cousin — a shift from the preceding unit's unnamed royal officials and general proposal-and-execution sequence (2:1-4) to the two individuals the rest of the book follows. This is a participant-introduction seam rather than a clause-type one: 2:1 itself opens with a fronted adjunct before its own qatal main verb, אַחַר֙ הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה כְּשֹׁ֕ךְ חֲמַ֖ת הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ זָכַ֤ר “After these things, when the wrath of King Ahasuerus was pacified, he remembered” web:Esth.2.1, and 2:3's proposal is a volitive weyiqtol inside quoted speech, וְיַפְקֵ֨ד הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ “Let the king appoint” web:Esth.2.3, not narrative wayyiqtol — while 2:7 itself opens with its own wayyiqtol, so grammatical mood alone does not separate 2:1-4 from 2:5-7. The background note on Mordecai and Esther ends before the plot resumes with a fresh participant return in 2:8.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 2:5-7 as a continuation of the courtiers' proposal would merge a stative background note into the wayyiqtol action sequence it does not belong to.

boundary_rationale: 2:8 reopens the scene of 2:3 through a cluster of verbal and locational echoes rather than a decree-language echo: the Susa-citadel setting אֶל שׁוּשַׁ֤ן web:Esth.2.3 recurs at אֶל שׁוּשַׁ֥ן web:Esth.2.8 (sweep: 2 book-wide: 2:3, 2:8), the custody construction אֶל יַ֥ד web:Esth.2.3 recurs at אֶל יַ֣ד web:Esth.2.8 (sweep: 3 book-wide: 2:3, 2:8, 2:14), the gathering root recurs in causative form (swept per attested spelling: וְיִקְבְּצ֣וּ “gather together” web:Esth.2.3, sweep: 1 book-wide, 2:3; וּֽבְהִקָּבֵ֞ץ “gathered together” web:Esth.2.8, sweep: 2 book-wide: 2:8, 2:19), and the custodian's name recurs alef-final הֵגֶ֛א at 2:3 and yod-final הֵגָ֑י at 2:8 — together marking the return to plot action after the character background of 2:5-7. The resumptive formula itself, וַיְהִ֗י בְּהִשָּׁמַ֤ע דְּבַר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְדָת֔וֹ “So, when the king's commandment and his decree was heard” web:Esth.2.8, carries the chapter's first dat (“decree”) token at form level (form-level dat sweep restricted to chapter 2 — optional prefix plus dat plus optional suffix: 2 verses, 2:8 and 2:12 — none earlier; a bare consonantal-string sweep over the same range reaches 4 by admitting the substring trap at 2:10 (מֽוֹלַדְתָּ֑הּ, already quoted above) and web:Esth.2.20 (מַגֶּ֤דֶת מֽוֹלַדְתָּהּ֙), both unrelated roots, not the dat noun); the noun is absent from 2:3, which uses the unrelated root paqad (“appoint”) instead. It opens the account of Esther's favor with Hegai, the concealment notice לֹא הִגִּ֣ידָה אֶסְתֵּ֔ר אֶת עַמָּ֖הּ וְאֶת מֽוֹלַדְתָּ֑הּ “Esther had not made known her people nor her relatives” web:Esth.2.10, and Mordecai's daily-vigil notice וּבְכָל י֣וֹם וָי֔וֹם מָרְדֳּכַי֙ מִתְהַלֵּ֔ךְ “Mordecai walked every day” web:Esth.2.11, which closes before the general ritual-procedure description opens at 2:12.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this span with the character introduction in 2:5-7 would collapse the stative-to-wayyiqtol seam marking the plot's resumption.

boundary_rationale: וּבְהַגִּ֡יעַ תֹּר֩ נַעֲרָ֨ה וְנַעֲרָ֜ה “Each young woman’s turn came” web:Esth.2.12 (turn-formula; the full four-word clause sweeps 1 book-wide at byte tier, occurring nowhere else pointed identically; its two-word opener וּבְהַגִּ֡יעַ תֹּר֩ sweeps 2 book-wide at the skeleton/consonantal tier, recurring only at 2:15 with different accentuation) opens a generalized, iterative description of the maidens’ purification cycle and nightly protocol, unattached to any named individual, running through the general rule לֹא תָב֥וֹא עוֹד֙ אֶל הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ כִּ֣י אִם חָפֵ֥ץ בָּ֛הּ הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ “She came in to the king no more, unless the king delighted in her” web:Esth.2.14; the same two-word opener recurs at the consonantal tier in 2:15 but there attached to Esther by name, marking the seam between the general rule and its specific application to her.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running this general description into Esther's specific turn at 2:15 would erase the formula-echo that distinguishes rule from instance.

boundary_rationale: וּבְהַגִּ֣יעַ תֹּר אֶסְתֵּ֣ר בַּת “Now when the turn of Esther, the daughter” web:Esth.2.15 reapplies the 2:12 turn-formula by name, opening Esther’s specific path to the crown, through the king’s love-notice וַיֶּאֱהַ֨ב הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֶת אֶסְתֵּר֙ מִכָּל הַנָּשִׁ֔ים “The king loved Esther more than all the women” web:Esth.2.17 and her coronation, to the double banquet notice מִשְׁתֶּ֣ה גָד֗וֹל לְכָל שָׂרָיו֙ וַעֲבָדָ֔יו אֵ֖ת מִשְׁתֵּ֣ה אֶסְתֵּ֑ר “a great feast for all his princes and his servants, even Esther’s feast” web:Esth.2.18, which alone among the mishteh-bearing verses carries two tokens of the mishteh string in one verse (form-level count, he-final, excluding the hishtaphel verb and the name Parmashta: sweep: 19 verses / 20 tokens book-wide; 2:18 is the sole verse with 2 tokens, all others carrying 1), before the seam to the obscure second-gathering notice at 2:19.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 2:15-16 and 2:17-18 as separate decisions would split one turn-to-coronation-to-feast sequence at no textual seam.

boundary_rationale: This span covers a genuinely low-confidence seam: the second-gathering notice וּבְהִקָּבֵ֥ץ בְּתוּל֖וֹת שֵׁנִ֑ית “When the virgins were gathered together the second time” web:Esth.2.19 has no clear antecedent once Esther's coronation already closed the gathering process in 2:16-18, and the 2:18|2:19 seam carries no tier-1 opener on its face. Two clauses report Mordecai at the gate — verse-final at 2:19, וּמָרְדֳּכַ֖י יֹשֵׁ֥ב בְּשַֽׁעַר הַמֶּֽלֶךְ “Mordecai was sitting in the king's gate” web:Esth.2.19, and verse-medial, immediately opening the resumed narration after the time formula at 2:21, וּמָרְדֳּכַ֖י יֹשֵׁ֣ב בְּשַֽׁעַר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ “while Mordecai was sitting in the king's gate” web:Esth.2.21 (the defective, vav-prefixed form of this clause sweeps 2 book-wide, at exactly 2:19 and 2:21; a plene-spelled participle predication of Mordecai at the gate recurs separately (sweep: 2 book-wide, 5:13 and 6:10) — יוֹשֵׁ֖ב בְּשַׁ֥עַר הַמֶּֽלֶךְ at 5:13 and הַיּוֹשֵׁ֖ב בְּשַׁ֣עַר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ at 6:10 — and is not part of this count). Read on its own, this resumptive repetition signals continuity — a frame clause interrupted by 2:20's concealment reminder אֵ֣ין אֶסְתֵּ֗ר מַגֶּ֤דֶת מֽוֹלַדְתָּהּ֙ “Esther had not yet made known her relatives” web:Esth.2.20 and then resumed — and by itself would argue for binding 2:19 through 2:21 into one continuous unit with 2:20 as a parenthetical aside, not for a boundary at the second occurrence. The seam at 2:20|2:21 instead rests on a different, genuinely tier-1 signal: the verse-initial time formula בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם “In those days” web:Esth.2.21 (sweep: 2 book-wide — 1:2, 2:21 — the only other instance being the exposition notice at 1:2), which marks 2:21 as opening fresh narrated material rather than merely resuming 2:19's frame. The SAMEKH mark follows 2:20 (oshb:Esth.2.20 (setumah, single-witness)), landing exactly at that seam as tier-3 corroboration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 2:19 backward to Esther's feast in 2:18 is equally arguable from the text alone and cannot be ruled out on tier-1 grounds.

boundary_rationale: The verse-initial time formula בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם “In those days” web:Esth.2.21 (sweep: 2 book-wide, the only other instance being the exposition notice at 1:2) opens fresh narrated material at 2:21, driving this span's opening boundary; the gate-clause report that follows it in the same verse, וּמָרְדֳּכַ֖י יֹשֵׁ֣ב בְּשַֽׁעַר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ “while Mordecai was sitting in the king's gate” web:Esth.2.21, is verse-medial here — an opener for the resumed narration, in contrast to its verse-final, closing position in 2:19 — and, read as a resumptive repetition with 2:19 alone, signals continuity across 2:20's parenthetical rather than driving a boundary at its own second occurrence; the boundary itself rests on the time formula, not on the repetition. Together they introduce the Bigthan-Teresh plot, which runs through the discovery-and-report chain to Mordecai, Esther, and the king (2:22) and closes with the chronicle-recording formula וַיִּכָּתֵ֗ב בְּסֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַיָּמִ֖ים לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ “it was written in the book of the chronicles in the king's presence” web:Esth.2.23 (this full clause sweeps 1 verse book-wide, 2:23 alone; the shorter, unprefixed phrase as it appears at 10:2, סֵ֨פֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י הַיָּמִ֔ים, sweeps 2 verses book-wide — 2:23, 10:2 — and the wider chronicle-phrase object, admitting 6:1's expanded form, sweeps 3 verses book-wide: 2:23, 6:1, 10:2). The PE mark follows 2:23 (oshb:Esth.2.23 (petuchah, single-witness)).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this notice into the preceding concealment reminder would overlook the verse-initial bayamim hahem formula that itself opens fresh narrated material at 2:21, independent of the gate-clause repetition.

boundary_rationale: אַחַ֣ר הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֗לֶּה גִּדַּל֩ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֜וֹשׁ אֶת הָמָ֧ן בֶּֽן הַמְּדָ֛תָא הָאֲגָגִ֖י וַֽיְנַשְּׂאֵ֑הוּ “After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him” web:Esth.3.1 (sweep: 2 book-wide for the "after these things" formula, the only other instance opening 2:1’s search-for-a-queen episode) opens a new temporal frame introducing Haman and the universal-homage decree, against which וּמָ֨רְדֳּכַ֔י לֹ֥א יִכְרַ֖ע וְלֹ֥א יִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֶֽה “But Mordecai didn’t bow down or pay him homage” web:Esth.3.2 sets the refusal that the gate-servants’ daily interrogation directly answers (3:3-4), closing when Mordecai discloses כִּֽי הִגִּ֥יד לָהֶ֖ם אֲשֶׁר ה֥וּא יְהוּדִֽי “for he had told them that he was a Jew” web:Esth.3.4 — the disclosure the servants then report to Haman, opening the next escalation. Ketiv/qere note: 3:4 spells "when they spoke" as ketiv באמרם against qere כְּאָמְרָ֤ם, disclosed because the verse is quoted here. 3:4's report of Mordecai's disclosure, וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ לְהָמָ֗ן “that they told Haman” web:Esth.3.4, and 3:6's citation of that same report as Haman's stated motive, כִּֽי הִגִּ֥ידוּ ל֖וֹ “for they had made known to him” web:Esth.3.6, share the plene-hifil higid family (sweep: 8 verses book-wide: 2:10, 3:4, 3:6, 4:4, 4:8, 4:12, 6:2, 8:1; 3:4 itself carries two tokens, וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ לְהָמָ֗ן and כִּֽי הִגִּ֥יד), and run as one unbroken report-to-motive chain across the 3:4|3:5 seam with no change of participant, place, or time. Three verses open with a temporal formula, each byte-verified verse-initial (1:3, 3:7, 9:1), explicitly not a single-string sweep: 3:7's verse-initial month-and-regnal-year formula בַּחֹ֤דֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן֙ הוּא חֹ֣דֶשׁ נִיסָ֔ן בִּשְׁנַת֙ שְׁתֵּ֣ים עֶשְׂרֵ֔ה לַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ “In the first month, which is the month Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus” web:Esth.3.7 stands among them as a materially tier-1 opener, corroborating the 3:6|3:7 seam over the 3:4|3:5 seam this span itself closes on.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the refusal in 3:1-2 from the interrogation that answers it in 3:3-4 would sever question from answer inside one continuous gate-scene.

boundary_rationale: Haman’s petition-speech opens with וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הָמָן֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ “Haman said to King Ahasuerus” web:Esth.3.8 and reaches the petition formula אִם עַל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֔וֹב יִכָּתֵ֖ב לְאַבְּדָ֑ם “If it pleases the king, let it be written that they be destroyed” web:Esth.3.9 (petition formula, sweep: 7 book-wide, second of the book’s seven instances), to which the king’s authorization responds in the same continuous exchange, handing over the signet ring וַיָּ֧סַר הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ אֶת טַבַּעְתּ֖וֹ מֵעַ֣ל יָד֑וֹ “The king took his ring from his hand” web:Esth.3.10 and the closing grant הַכֶּ֖סֶף נָת֣וּן לָ֑ךְ וְהָעָ֕ם לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת בּ֖וֹ כַּטּ֥וֹב בְּעֵינֶֽיךָ “The silver is given to you, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you” web:Esth.3.11; no scene, participant, or day-marker separates request from response before the scribes-summons formula opens the edict inset at 3:12.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting a decision at 3:9|3:10 would separate a petition from its answer within one unbroken audience before the king.

boundary_rationale: The scribes-summons formula וַיִּקָּרְאוּ֩ סֹפְרֵ֨י הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ “Then the king’s scribes were called in” web:Esth.3.12 (sweep: 2 book-wide, the deliberate counter-edict parallel at 8:9) opens the inset, staying with its dispatch (3:13, addressed לְהַשְׁמִ֡יד לַהֲרֹ֣ג וּלְאַבֵּ֣ד אֶת כָּל הַ֠יְּהוּדִים “to destroy, to kill, and to cause to perish, all Jews” web:Esth.3.13) and publication (3:14) through its narrative-frame reaction verse: הָֽרָצִ֞ים יָצְא֤וּ דְחוּפִים֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְהַדָּ֥ת נִתְּנָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֑ה “The couriers went out in haste by the king’s commandment, and the decree was given out in the citadel of Susa” web:Esth.3.15 opens the verse, its middle clause pivots to the king and Haman's ironic ease, וְהַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ יָשְׁב֣וּ לִשְׁתּ֔וֹת “The king and Haman sat down to drink” web:Esth.3.15, and it closes on the city's alarm, וְהָעִ֥יר שׁוּשָׁ֖ן נָבֽוֹכָה “the city of Susa was perplexed” web:Esth.3.15 — three clauses inside one verse that cannot be split apart: the couriers' dispatch, the throne's complacency, and the streets' distress read as a single ironic beat, which 4:1's mourning directly answers. 4:1 opens a hard participant shift onto Mordecai alone, וּמָרְדֳּכַ֗י יָדַע֙ אֶת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֣ר נַעֲשָׂ֔ה “Now when Mordecai found out all that was done” web:Esth.4.1, moving outside the citadel into the city and into mourning ritual, וַיֵּצֵא֙ בְּת֣וֹךְ הָעִ֔יר וַיִּזְעַ֛ק זְעָקָ֥ה גְדֹלָ֖ה וּמָרָֽה “went out into the middle of the city, and wailed loudly and bitterly” web:Esth.4.1 — a scene, location, and participant break from the drinking king and the perplexed city that closes 3:15, with no narrative continuity carrying across the seam except Mordecai’s discovery of events, which itself opens a new information-relay unit rather than continuing this one. The PE mark follows 3:15 (oshb:Esth.3.15 (petuchah, single-witness)), landing exactly at this seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Severing 3:15's reaction clause from the edict that provokes it would split one verse's own three-clause sequence — dispatch, royal ease, civic alarm — apart from itself.

boundary_rationale: The preceding scene ends with the court at ease: “The king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city of Susa was perplexed” (web:Esth.3.15), a clause built on וְהַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ יָשְׁב֣וּ לִשְׁתּ֔וֹת וְהָעִ֥יר שׁוּשָׁ֖ן נָבֽוֹכָה, the king and Haman as joint subject of a leisure verb. The new span opens on a fronted, contrastive subject — וּמָרְדֳּכַ֗י יָדַע֙ אֶת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֣ר נַעֲשָׂ֔ה, literally "and Mordecai knew all that was done" — reversing both the grammatical subject and the register: drinking gives way to grief, and the verse's own opening vav marks the pivot rather than a mere continuation. The WEB renders this “Now when Mordecai found out all that was done, Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth with ashes, and went out into the middle of the city, and wailed loudly and bitterly” (web:Esth.4.1). Esth.4.2 keeps the same subject and location (Mordecai at the gate) before Esth.4.3 opens a distributive formula, “In every province, wherever the king's commandment and his decree came, there was great mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping, and wailing” (web:Esth.4.3), generalizing Mordecai's individual mourning into a province-wide notice — the same distributive shift from a single actor to an empire-wide report recurs at the joy notice that closes this part (Esth.8.17). The shared consonantal string underlying both the noun at Esth.4.3 and the imperative verb at Esth.4.16 is attested at exactly 2 verses book-wide, sweep: 2 (Esth.4.3 the noun, Esth.4.16 the imperative verb), so the mourning-fast pairing introduced here is picked up again within the same chapter. The fasting NOUN itself, tracked apart from that string, is a separate object at sweep: 2 (Esth.4.3; Esth.9.31 in the defective plural, unreachable by the string sweep since that spelling drops the vav) — so the same term that opens the mourning here is also the term the Purim institution later commemorates: “as they had imposed upon themselves and their descendants in the matter of the fastings and their mourning” (web:Esth.9.31). A petuchah closes the prior scene at Esth.3.15 (petuchah, single-witness); it is tier-3 corroboration for the seam, not its driver — the subject and register reversal is.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping 4:1-3 fused to the edict's closing scene ignores the change from the king and Haman's leisure at 3:15 to Mordecai's grief in the street.

boundary_rationale: The scene shifts from the city gate to the palace: וַ֠תָּבוֹאינָה נַעֲר֨וֹת אֶסְתֵּ֤ר וְסָרִיסֶ֨יהָ֙ וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ לָ֔הּ, "Esther's maidens and her eunuchs came and told her" — a new participant set and location, WEB “Esther's maidens and her eunuchs came and told her this, and the queen was exceedingly grieved” (web:Esth.4.4). Esther's own failed gesture — clothing sent, “but he didn't receive it” (web:Esth.4.4) — triggers her dispatch of a named intermediary in Esth.4.5-6, who then carries Mordecai's report in Esth.4.7-8 and returns it to her in Esth.4.9, closing with וַיָּב֖וֹא הֲתָ֑ךְ וַיַּגֵּ֣ד לְאֶסְתֵּ֔ר אֵ֖ת דִּבְרֵ֥י מָרְדֳּכָֽי, "Hathach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai" — WEB “Hathach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai” (web:Esth.4.9). The whole span is one bracketed fact-finding cycle: it opens with Esther learning secondhand and closes with her learning firsthand (via Hathach) exactly what Mordecai wants her to do, a closed messenger loop rather than a resting point mid-errand.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 4:4 as its own decision would sever the maidens' report from the very inquiry it triggers.

boundary_rationale: A second relay cycle opens with its own speech-formula: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר אֶסְתֵּר֙ לַהֲתָ֔ךְ וַתְּצַוֵּ֖הוּ אֶֽל מָרְדֳּכָֽי, "Then Esther spoke to Hathach, and commanded him to Mordecai" — WEB “Then Esther spoke to Hathach, and gave him a message to Mordecai” (web:Esth.4.10), introducing the content of Esth.4.11 (the law of unbidden entry, closing “I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days.” web:Esth.4.11). The cycle closes with the delivery notice וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ לְמָרְדֳּכָ֔י אֵ֖ת דִּבְרֵ֥י אֶסְתֵּֽר in full, WEB “They told Esther's words to Mordecai” (web:Esth.4.12) — the same dispatch-then-delivery shape as the earlier Hathach cycle (Esth.4.5-Esth.4.9), now run in the opposite direction (Esther to Mordecai rather than Mordecai to Esther). A petuchah closes the verse, oshb:Esth.4.12 (petuchah, single-witness); tier-3 corroboration for a seam already driven by the completed delivery formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A backward merge into the preceding cycle is rejected because no mark falls at Esth.4.9 or Esth.4.10 and Esth.4.5-9 dispatches Esther's inquiry and returns with Mordecai's report while Esth.4.10-12 dispatches Esther's own reply-content to Mordecai, a fresh outgoing message rather than a continuation of the same errand, so the seam holds on content and direction alone.

boundary_rationale: Mordecai's reply opens with direct quoted content rather than a further third-person delivery notice: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר מָרְדֳּכַ֖י לְהָשִׁ֣יב אֶל אֶסְתֵּ֑ר, literally "Mordecai said, to cause word to be brought back to Esther" — WEB “Then Mordecai asked them to return this answer to Esther:” (web:Esth.4.13). The infinitive here (le-hashiv, "to cause to be brought back") is causative and names an unspecified relaying agency, exactly as the matched infinitive does two verses later at Esther's own reply (Esth.4.15) — so the relay itself is mediated in both directions, not unmediated at Esth.4.13 alone. What distinguishes this verse from the preceding delivery notice at Esth.4.12 (וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ לְמָרְדֳּכָ֔י אֵ֖ת דִּבְרֵ֥י אֶסְתֵּֽר, WEB “They told Esther's words to Mordecai.” (web:Esth.4.12)) is that Esth.4.13 supplies quoted content — the "who knows" appeal of Esth.4.14 — rather than merely reporting that a message arrived. Esther's reply opens with the matched formula וַתֹּ֥אמֶר אֶסְתֵּ֖ר לְהָשִׁ֥יב אֶֽל מָרְדֳּכָֽי in full, WEB “Then Esther asked them to answer Mordecai” (web:Esth.4.15) — the same infinitive "to reply" (le-hashiv) used of Mordecai in Esth.4.13, now applied to Esther, a chiastic pairing of response-formulas that binds Esth.4.13-17 together as one challenge-and-resolution exchange, closing with her decision (“and if I perish, I perish.” web:Esth.4.16) and Mordecai's compliance (web:Esth.4.17). This span sits between two marks: a petuchah already closes the preceding relay at Esth.4.12 (petuchah, single-witness), and a setumah closes this one at Esth.4.17 (setumah, single-witness) — both tier-3 corroboration, framing but not driving a boundary set by the matched response-formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating 4:15-17 from Mordecai's preceding challenge would strand Esther's answer from the objection it answers.

boundary_rationale: A fresh temporal formula opens the chapter: וַיְהִ֣י בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֗י, "Now it happened on the third day" — WEB “Now on the third day, Esther put on her royal clothing...” (web:Esth.5.1), counting out the fast just vowed at “fast for me...three days, night or day” (web:Esth.4.16) and moving from private resolve to public act. The audience is granted in Esth.5.2 (scepter extended, favor found), the king's open-ended offer follows in Esth.5.3, and Esther's actual request — an invitation to a banquet — closes the unit in Esth.5.4-5, foreshadowing the invitation-formula echo at Esth.5.8. This span holds together as the approach-through-first-invitation movement, ending once king and Haman are seated (“So the king and Haman came to the banquet that Esther had prepared.” web:Esth.5.5). A setumah already closed the preceding dialogue at Esth.4.17 (setumah, single-witness); this scene carries its own setumah at Esth.5.2 (setumah, single-witness) marking the scepter-grant — both disclosed as corroboration, neither driving the seam set by the day-formula opener.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Halting this unit at 5:2 alone would cut the scepter-grant away from the royal offer it provokes.

boundary_rationale: At the banquet itself the king restates his open offer: מַה שְּׁאֵלָתֵ֖ךְ וְיִנָּ֣תֵֽן לָ֑ךְ וּמַה בַּקָּשָׁתֵ֛ךְ עַד חֲצִ֥י הַמַּלְכ֖וּת וְתֵעָֽשׂ — WEB “What is your petition? It shall be granted you. What is your request? Even to the half of the kingdom it shall be performed.” (web:Esth.5.6). Esth.5.3's own question is already two-part and already carries the identical half-kingdom clause (מַה לָּ֖ךְ אֶסְתֵּ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֑ה וּמַה בַּקָּשָׁתֵ֛ךְ עַד חֲצִ֥י הַמַּלְכ֖וּת וְיִנָּ֥תֵֽן לָֽךְ, 11 tokens across two members); Esth.5.6 restates it in 10 tokens, also two members, byte-identical in its second member (וּמַה בַּקָּשָׁתֵ֛ךְ עַד חֲצִ֥י הַמַּלְכ֖וּת), sweep: 3 book-wide for that exact clause (Esth.5.3, Esth.5.6, Esth.7.2) — a resequencing of the same two-part structure, not an expansion, and the half-kingdom offer is not new here. This banquet-of-wine refrain reopens the request rather than continuing the approach scene, and the same doubled formula recurs at Esth.7.2 when the second banquet reaches its own turning point. Esther defers again in Esth.5.7-8, closing on two petition formulas placed back to back: אִם מָצָ֨אתִי חֵ֜ן בְּעֵינֵ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ וְאִם עַל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ ט֔וֹב לָתֵת֙ אֶת שְׁאֵ֣לָתִ֔י וְלַעֲשׂ֖וֹת אֶת בַּקָּשָׁתִ֑י יָב֧וֹא הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ וְהָמָ֗ן אֶל הַמִּשְׁתֶּה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֣ה לָהֶ֔ם וּמָחָ֥ר אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֖ה כִּדְבַ֥ר הַמֶּֽלֶךְ, WEB “If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it pleases the king to grant my petition and to perform my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I will prepare for them, and I will do tomorrow as the king has said.” (web:Esth.5.8) — the im-matzati-chen ("if I have found favor") formula, sweep: 3 book-wide (Esth.5.8, Esth.7.3, Esth.8.5), immediately followed by the im-al-hamelekh-tov ("if it pleases the king") formula, sweep: 7 book-wide (Esth.1.19, Esth.3.9, Esth.5.4, Esth.5.8, Esth.7.3, Esth.8.5, Esth.9.13) — two distinct formulas naming two different counts, not one.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Absorbing 5:6-8 into the preceding audience scene would erase the banquet-of-wine refrain that reopens the petition.

boundary_rationale: Scene and mood both turn: וַיֵּצֵ֤א הָמָן֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא שָׂמֵ֖חַ וְט֣וֹב לֵ֑ב, "Then Haman went out that day, joyful and glad of heart" — WEB “Then Haman went out that day joyful and glad of heart, but when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate...he was filled with wrath” (web:Esth.5.9), moving the setting from the banquet hall to the gate and then to Haman's own house, and the participants from the royal party to Haman's household. His boast to Zeresh and his friends (Esth.5.10-12) is immediately undercut in his own words, “Yet all this avails me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate” (web:Esth.5.13), and Zeresh's counsel to build a gallows closes the unit: "and this thing pleased Haman, and he made the gallows" — WEB “This pleased Haman, so he had the gallows made” (web:Esth.5.14), וַיִּיטַ֧ב הַדָּבָ֛ר לִפְנֵ֥י הָמָ֖ן וַיַּ֥עַשׂ הָעֵֽץ. The fifty-cubit gallows built here becomes the very structure named again at Esth.7.9-10, so this scene, though short, is a self-contained cause set into motion rather than the tail of the banquet scene that precedes it. A petuchah closes the verse, oshb:Esth.5.14 (petuchah, single-witness); Writings marks are tier-3 at most and cannot themselves decide whether this venting-and-counsel scene stands alone or closes the banquet unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 5:9-14 into the first banquet's close would attach Haman's private humiliation to a scene he has already left.

boundary_rationale: A new night and a new cause open the pivot chapter: בַּלַּ֣יְלָה הַה֔וּא נָדְדָ֖ה שְׁנַ֣ת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ, "On that night, the sleep of the king fled" — WEB “On that night, the king couldn't sleep. He commanded the book of records of the chronicles to be brought” (web:Esth.6.1), naming the chronicle-frame phrase סֵ֤פֶר הַזִּכְרֹנוֹת֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י הַיָּמִ֔ים in its fullest form; the same source-notice recurs in shorter form at Esth.2.23 and Esth.10.2, sweep: 3 book-wide for the phrase "the book of the chronicles" in any of its three forms. The reading turns up Mordecai's unrewarded loyalty (Esth.6.2-3), and the king's follow-up question, “Who is in the court?” (web:Esth.6.4), is answered in the same verse by a disjunctive waw-fronted-subject clause naming Haman's arrival at a lexically marked location: וְהָמָ֣ן בָּ֗א לַחֲצַ֤ר בֵּית הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ הַחִ֣יצוֹנָ֔ה, “Haman had come into the outer court of the king’s house” (web:Esth.6.4) — the only occurrence of the qualified "outer" court in the book, sweep: 1 (Esth.6.4), against the qualified "inner" court at sweep: 2 (Esth.4.11, Esth.5.1), the only other qualified court term in the book. That locative clause is circumstantial background answering the king's own question, not a scene-opening device on the model of Esth.4.1: no register or topic shift accompanies it, and the interrogation about honoring Mordecai runs uninterrupted across the seam into the servants' answer at Esth.6.5. Haman's private assumption that the honor must be meant for him, “Who would the king delight to honor more than myself?” (web:Esth.6.6), closes the unit on the edge of dramatic irony rather than at a scene change. His script runs through Esth.6.9, and the king's reply reverses it in the same breath: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ לְהָמָ֗ן מַ֠הֵר קַ֣ח אֶת הַלְּב֤וּשׁ, "Then the king said to Haman, 'hurry, take the clothing'" — WEB “Then the king said to Haman, “Hurry and take the clothing and the horse, as you have said,” (web:Esth.6.10). boundary_rationale: The two men part ways in the same verse: וַיָּ֥שָׁב מָרְדֳּכַ֖י אֶל שַׁ֣עַר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ נִדְחַ֣ף אֶל בֵּית֔וֹ אָבֵ֖ל וַחֲפ֥וּי רֹֽאשׁ in full, WEB “Mordecai came back to the king's gate, but Haman hurried to his house, mourning and having his head covered” (web:Esth.6.12) — Mordecai returns to his fixed post while Haman flees home in the posture of a mourner. The covering-root itself is a two-point book-wide device, sweep: 2 (Esth.6.12, Esth.7.8) — no third occurrence exists, and none falls at Esth.4.1, where Mordecai's own grief is marked instead by torn clothes and sackcloth and ashes (web:Esth.4.1), a related but textually distinct mourning register. The head covered here at Esth.6.12 is answered by Haman's own face covered later at Esth.7.8, when the king's word condemns him — the covering-root's two attested spellings in the book, וַחֲפ֥וּי (Esth.6.12) and חָפֽוּ (Esth.7.8), with no third occurrence. That echo crosses this span's own back seam at Esth.6.14|Esth.7.1 and reaches past it into the following unit; disclosed here as a forward-pointing continuity signal rather than a cohesion driver internal to Esth.6.12-Esth.6.14. Only the SPEAKING roster narrows: Esth.6.13's counsel is voiced by “Then his wise men and Zeresh his wife said to him,” (web:Esth.6.13) (וַיֹּ֩אמְרוּ֩ ל֨וֹ חֲכָמָ֜יו וְזֶ֣רֶשׁ אִשְׁתּ֗וֹ) — חֲכָמָ֜יו, "his wise men" attested nowhere else in the book, sweep: 1 (Esth.6.13) — replacing the collective “all his friends” as speakers while the wider household stays the same audience. It is that household's own prior counsel that reverses here: “If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of Jewish descent, you will not prevail against him, but you will surely fall before him.” (web:Esth.6.13). The chapter's last verse then breaks off the fatalistic scene mid-conversation: עוֹדָם֙ מְדַבְּרִ֣ים עִמּ֔וֹ וְסָרִיסֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ הִגִּ֑יעוּ וַיַּבְהִ֨לוּ֙ לְהָבִ֣יא אֶת הָמָ֔ן אֶל הַמִּשְׁתֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁר עָשְׂתָ֥ה אֶסְתֵּֽר — WEB “While they were yet talking with him, the king's eunuchs came, and hurried to bring Haman to the banquet that Esther had prepared.” (web:Esth.6.14). This closing clause is the low-confidence hinge into the next scene: the next material opens “So the king and Haman came to banquet with Esther the queen” (web:Esth.7.1) with no new time formula and no fresh introduction of the banquet, reading as the direct continuation of the "hurried" summons rather than a fresh scene-opener in its own right. boundary_rationale: The banquet notice that closed the last chapter's hurried summons is realized in one line, “So the king and Haman came to banquet with Esther the queen” (web:Esth.7.1), and the king repeats the doubled petition-formula, also “on the second day at the banquet of wine, “What is your petition, queen Esther?” (web:Esth.7.2): גַּ֣ם בַּיּ֤וֹם הַשֵּׁנִי֙ בְּמִשְׁתֵּ֣ה הַיַּ֔יִן מַה שְּׁאֵלָתֵ֛ךְ אֶסְתֵּ֥ר הַמַּלְכָּ֖ה, the same doubled question-formula already met at Esth.5.6 — paired at the consonantal tier, skeleton sweep: 3 book-wide (Esth.5.6, Esth.7.2, Esth.9.12; the pairing unifies only at the skeleton tier, not byte-for-byte); this occurrence is the second of the three. Esther finally names her petitioner as her people and her opponent as Haman across Esth.7.3-6. The king's fury then drives him out and back within the same confrontation: וְהַמֶּ֜לֶךְ קָ֤ם בַּחֲמָתוֹ֙ מִמִּשְׁתֵּ֣ה הַיַּ֔יִן אֶל גִּנַּ֖ת הַבִּיתָ֑ן וְהָמָ֣ן עָמַ֗ד לְבַקֵּ֤שׁ עַל נַפְשׁוֹ֙ מֵֽאֶסְתֵּ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה כִּ֣י רָאָ֔ה כִּֽי כָלְתָ֥ה אֵלָ֛יו הָרָעָ֖ה מֵאֵ֥ת הַמֶּֽלֶךְ, “The king arose in his wrath from the banquet of wine and went into the palace garden. Haman stood up to make request for his life to Esther the queen, for he saw that there was evil determined against him by the king.” (web:Esth.7.7), then וְהַמֶּ֡לֶךְ שָׁב֩ מִגִּנַּ֨ת הַבִּיתָ֜ן אֶל בֵּ֣ית מִשְׁתֵּ֣ה הַיַּ֗יִן וְהָמָן֙ נֹפֵ֔ל עַל הַמִּטָּה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אֶסְתֵּ֣ר עָלֶ֔יהָ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ הֲ֠גַם לִכְבּ֧וֹשׁ אֶת הַמַּלְכָּ֛ה עִמִּ֖י בַּבָּ֑יִת הַדָּבָ֗ר יָצָא֙ מִפִּ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וּפְנֵ֥י הָמָ֖ן חָפֽוּ, “Then the king returned out of the palace garden into the place of the banquet of wine; and Haman had fallen on the couch where Esther was. Then the king said, “Will he even assault the queen in front of me in the house?” As the word went out of the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face.” (web:Esth.7.8) — an explicit exit and return between two named locations, the articled "garden of the pavilion" locative attested at exactly 2 verses book-wide at the consonantal tier, skeleton sweep: 2 (Esth.7.7, Esth.7.8), both interior to this span — the bare garden noun itself recurs a third time at Esth.1.5 in its unarticled construction, echoic of the book's opening banquet setting but outside this span — and the banquet-of-wine locative, skeleton sweep: 4 book-wide (Esth.5.6, Esth.7.2, Esth.7.7, Esth.7.8), three of them interior. The unit holds together not because no movement occurs but because the movement is contained within one ongoing confrontation: no new participant enters, no resolution is reached mid-transit, and the king returns to find Haman still fallen at the same couch, closing on וּפְנֵ֥י הָמָ֖ן חָפֽוּ, "and Haman's face was covered" — the covering-root's two attested spellings in the book, וַחֲפ֥וּי (Esth.6.12) and חָפֽוּ (Esth.7.8), with no third occurrence — now predicated of his face rather than his head as it was there. A setumah falls at Esth.7.4 (setumah, single-witness), interior to this span, and another at Esth.7.8 (setumah, single-witness), at the seam Esth.7.8|Esth.7.9 which is this span's own closing edge; neither is treated as the driver of any internal seam.

boundary_rationale: A background figure steps forward to speak: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר חַ֠רְבוֹנָה אֶחָ֨ד מִן הַסָּרִיסִ֜ים לִפְנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ גַּ֣ם הִנֵּה הָעֵ֣ץ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂ֪ה הָמָ֟ן לְֽמָרְדֳּכַ֞י אֲשֶׁ֧ר דִּבֶּר ט֣וֹב עַל הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ עֹמֵד֙ בְּבֵ֣ית הָמָ֔ן גָּבֹ֖הַּ חֲמִשִּׁ֣ים אַמָּ֑ה וַיֹּ֥אמֶר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ תְּלֻ֥הוּ עָלָֽיו — WEB “Then Harbonah, one of the eunuchs who were with the king, said, "Behold, the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman has made for Mordecai, who spoke good for the king, is standing at Haman's house." The king said, "Hang him on it!"” (web:Esth.7.9). This is the same eunuch listed among the seven who attend the king: לִ֠מְהוּמָן בִּזְּתָ֨א חַרְבוֹנָ֜א בִּגְתָ֤א וַאֲבַגְתָא֙ זֵתַ֣ר וְכַרְכַּ֔ס שִׁבְעַת֙ הַסָּ֣רִיסִ֔ים הַמְשָׁ֣רְתִ֔ים אֶת פְּנֵ֖י הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ, WEB “Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcass, the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king,” (web:Esth.1.10) — one item in a seven-member list there, with no speaking part. His name is attested at exactly 2 verses book-wide across two consonantal spellings, sweep: 1 for the Esth.1.10 form and sweep: 1 for the Esth.7.9 form, and this is the only one of the two where he speaks; his reactivation as an actor here is the scene-internal signal, not a claim that the name is new to the book. He names the very gallows built at Esth.5.14. The king's one-line order and its execution close the confrontation: וַיִּתְלוּ֙ אֶת הָמָ֔ן עַל הָעֵ֖ץ אֲשֶׁר הֵכִ֣ין לְמָרְדֳּכָ֑י וַחֲמַ֥ת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ שָׁכָֽכָה in full, WEB “So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the king's wrath was pacified” (web:Esth.7.10) — a resolution notice ("the king's wrath was pacified") that answers the anger that opened the confrontation at Esth.7.7 and gives the unit its own closure distinct from the accusation scene that precedes it. A setumah already closed Esth.7.8 (setumah, single-witness) at the front seam of this span, and a petuchah closes Esth.7.10 (petuchah, single-witness) at its end; both disclosed together, with Harbonah's reactivation as speaker treated as the actual driver of the seam.

boundary_rationale: A dated summary notice opens the new chapter in the third person: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא נָתַ֞ן הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ֙ לְאֶסְתֵּ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה, "On that day, King Ahasuerus gave to Esther the queen" — WEB “On that day, King Ahasuerus gave the house of Haman, the Jews' enemy, to Esther the queen” (web:Esth.8.1), reporting a property transfer as a completed act rather than staging a new appeal in direct speech. Esth.8.2 continues the same summary register — the ring transferred, Mordecai set over Haman's house — with no quoted speech anywhere in either verse. This closed, narrated notice is distinct in kind from the personal, tearful audience that opens immediately after it: “Esther spoke yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet and begged him with tears” (web:Esth.8.3). A petuchah already closed the previous scene at Esth.7.10 (petuchah, single-witness), and another closes this one at Esth.8.2 (petuchah, single-witness); both disclosed as corroboration for a boundary driven by the shift from narrated summary to direct, embodied appeal.

boundary_rationale: Esther returns to direct, embodied speech: וַתּ֣וֹסֶף אֶסְתֵּ֗ר וַתְּדַבֵּר֙ לִפְנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַתִּפֹּ֖ל לִפְנֵ֣י רַגְלָ֑יו וַתֵּ֣בְךְּ וַתִּתְחַנֶּן ל֗וֹ, "Esther again spoke before the king, and fell before his feet, and wept, and begged him" — WEB “Esther spoke yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet and begged him with tears to put away the mischief of Haman the Agagite” (web:Esth.8.3), a bodily and emotional register (falling, weeping) absent from the narrated transfer notice that precedes it. Her formal request follows in Esth.8.4-5, and the unit closes on her own rhetorical question: כִּ֠י אֵיכָכָ֤ה אוּכַל֙ וְֽרָאִ֔יתִי בָּרָעָ֖ה אֲשֶׁר יִמְצָ֣א אֶת עַמִּ֑י, "For how can I endure, and see the evil that would find my people" — WEB “For how can I endure to see the evil that would come to my people? How can I endure to see the destruction of my relatives?” (web:Esth.8.6). A petuchah already closed the transfer notice at Esth.8.2 (petuchah, single-witness), and a setumah closes this appeal at Esth.8.6 (setumah, single-witness); both disclosed together as corroboration for a boundary driven by the change of register.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The royal audience and both petitioners are continuous across Esth.8.1-2|8.3 — no verse records the king dismissing or the petitioners departing and returning — so attaching Esther's renewed appeal to the transfer notice that precedes it is not ruled out by any break in audience; it is rejected instead because the two spans differ in speech-act register: Esth.8.1-2 narrates a completed grant in the third person with no quoted speech, while Esth.8.3 opens Esther's own embodied, tearful direct address — a register shift internal to one continuous audience rather than a change of scene.

boundary_rationale: A new speaker answers, and answers two people at once: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֹשׁ֙ לְאֶסְתֵּ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה וּֽלְמָרְדֳּכַ֖י הַיְּהוּדִ֑י, "Then King Ahasuerus said to Esther the queen and to Mordecai the Jew" — WEB “Then King Ahasuerus said to Esther the queen and to Mordecai the Jew, “See, I have given Esther the house of Haman,” (web:Esth.8.7). Mordecai has taken no speaking part since his reply relayed at Esth.4.13 — the string וַיֹּ֥אמֶר מָרְדֳּכַ֖י, "Mordecai said," his only speech-introducing occurrence book-wide, sweep: 1 (Esth.4.13) — and his reintroduction here as a direct addressee, alongside Esther, marks a participant shift distinct from Esther's solo appeal in the preceding verses. The king's reply authorizes rather than grants outright: “Write also to the Jews as it pleases you, in the king’s name, and seal it with the king’s ring” (web:Esth.8.8), closing on the irreversibility formula כִּֽי כְתָ֞ב אֲשֶׁר נִכְתָּ֣ב בְּשֵׁם הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ וְנַחְתּ֛וֹם בְּטַבַּ֥עַת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֵ֥ין לְהָשִֽׁיב, "for a writing that is written in the king's name and sealed with the king's ring, there is no reversing" — the same writing-and-sealing-in-the-king's-name apparatus already used at the original edict's close, Esth.3.12 (בְּשֵׁ֨ם הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֹשׁ֙ נִכְתָּ֔ב וְנֶחְתָּ֖ם בְּטַבַּ֥עַת הַמֶּֽלֶךְ), which shares the signet noun with this verse, sweep: 5 verses, 6 tokens book-wide (Esth.3.10, Esth.3.12, Esth.8.2, Esth.8.8, Esth.8.10; Esth.8.8 itself carries two); the decree noun itself is a separate object, absent from both this verse and Esth.3.12, and attested instead at Esth.1.19 among the wider decree-noun count, sweep: 20 tokens over 19 verses book-wide.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 8:7-8 as part of Esther's speech misassigns the king's own reply, addressed to Mordecai as much as to her.

boundary_rationale: The counter-edict opens with the same scribes-summons formula used of the original edict: וַיִּקָּרְא֣וּ סֹפְרֵֽי הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ בָּֽעֵת הַ֠הִיא, "Then the king's scribes were called at that time" — WEB “Then the king's scribes were called at that time, in the third month, which is the month Sivan” (web:Esth.8.9), matching וַיִּקָּרְאוּ֩ סֹפְרֵ֨י הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ at Esth.3.12 in substance though not letter for letter — the two pointed strings differ (byte sweep: 0, accent_stripped sweep: 0) and match only once points are stripped, skeleton sweep: 2 (Esth.3.12, Esth.8.9) — a deliberate edict/counter-edict pairing at the consonantal tier. The same verse repeats the merism, here מֵהֹ֣דּוּ וְעַד כּ֗וּשׁ, "from India to Cush" — in substance though not letter for letter against its Esth.1.1 form, מֵהֹ֣דּוּ וְעַד כּ֔וּשׁ: the two occurrences differ only in the cantillation of the final word (byte sweep: 0) — found at exactly 2 verses book-wide once cantillation is stripped, accent_stripped sweep: 2 (Esth.1.1, Esth.8.9), tying the counter-edict's geographic scope back to the book's opening frame. The inset runs through the date-setting (Esth.8.12) and publication (Esth.8.13) to its own dispatch notice, closing הָרָצִ֞ים רֹכְבֵ֤י הָרֶ֨כֶשׁ֙ הָֽאֲחַשְׁתְּרָנִ֔ים יָֽצְא֛וּ מְבֹהָלִ֥ים וּדְחוּפִ֖ים בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וְהַדָּ֥ת נִתְּנָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֥ן הַבִּירָֽה in full, WEB “So the couriers who rode on royal horses went out, hastened and pressed on by the king's commandment. The decree was given out in the citadel of Susa” (web:Esth.8.14), which echoes the closing clause of the first edict's dispatch notice at Esth.3.15 in substance though not letter for letter (the pointing differs where each clause sits differently inside its own sentence). This document inset stays with its narrative frame as a single unit, paralleling the edict block at Esth.3.12-15, and is not subdivided internally; a petuchah closes it at Esth.8.14 (petuchah, single-witness), disclosed as corroboration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the counter-edict at its date clause would sever 8:12 from the authorization it depends on.

boundary_rationale: The legal register of the edict gives way to a scene of public reception: וּמָרְדֳּכַ֞י יָצָ֣א מִלִּפְנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ בִּלְב֤וּשׁ מַלְכוּת֙ תְּכֵ֣לֶת וָח֔וּר וַעֲטֶ֤רֶת זָהָב֙ גְּדוֹלָ֔ה וְתַכְרִ֥יךְ בּ֖וּץ וְאַרְגָּמָ֑ן וְהָעִ֣יר שׁוּשָׁ֔ן צָהֲלָ֖ה וְשָׂמֵֽחָה, "And Mordecai went out from before the king in royal clothing" — WEB “Mordecai went out of the presence of the king in royal clothing of blue and white...and the city of Susa shouted and was glad” (web:Esth.8.15), naming Susa specifically rather than the provinces generally. Esth.8.16 then summarizes the reaction for "the Jews" as a people rather than the city: לַיְּהוּדִ֕ים הָֽיְתָ֥ה אוֹרָ֖ה וְשִׂמְחָ֑ה וְשָׂשֹׂ֖ן וִיקָֽר in full, WEB “The Jews had light, gladness, joy, and honor” (web:Esth.8.16), carrying the simchah NOUN at chirik-sheva vocalization: sweep: 6 book-wide, 7 tokens (Esth.8.16, Esth.8.17, Esth.9.17, Esth.9.18, Esth.9.19, Esth.9.22 x2). The preceding verse's own וְשָׂמֵֽחָה, "was glad" (oshb:Esth.8.15), names a distinct object, the simchah ADJECTIVE at qamets-tsere vocalization — consonantally identical to the noun but pointed apart: sweep: 3 book-wide (Esth.5.9, Esth.5.14, Esth.8.15). Naming the wider ROOT that covers both forms together: sweep: 9 book-wide, 10 tokens. This local, Susa-and-the-Jews notice is bounded by the legal document that precedes it and by the empire-wide distributive report that follows it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying 8:15-16 forward into the province-wide notice would flatten the difference between Susa's local celebration and the empire-wide report that follows.

boundary_rationale: The verse opens its own distributive formula, doubling both terms of scope: וּבְכָל מְדִינָ֨ה וּמְדִינָ֜ה וּבְכָל עִ֣יר וָעִ֗יר, "and in every province and province, and in every city and city" — WEB “In every province and in every city, wherever the king's commandment and his decree came, the Jews had gladness, joy, a feast and a holiday” (web:Esth.8.17). That doubled medinah-umedinah shape occurs at 8 verses book-wide, sweep: 8 book-wide (Esth.1.22, Esth.3.12, Esth.3.14, Esth.4.3, Esth.8.9, Esth.8.13, Esth.8.17, Esth.9.28), the same formula that opened this part's own mourning notice at Esth.4.3, closing the circle it began. The verse ends on its own resolution clause, “for the fear of the Jews had fallen on them” (web:Esth.8.17), and adds a notice found nowhere else in the book: מִֽתְיַהֲדִ֔ים, "became Jews", sweep: 1 book-wide for that verb form (Esth.8.17 only). The next material opens on an entirely different formula, a specific calendar date rather than a summary report: “Now in the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the month” (web:Esth.9.1), וּבִשְׁנֵים֩ עָשָׂ֨ר חֹ֜דֶשׁ הוּא חֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֗ר בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁ֨ה עָשָׂ֥ר יוֹם֙ — a fresh day-by-day narrative beginning rather than a continuation of the present-tense, empire-wide summary that Esth.8.17 completes. No paragraph mark falls at either edge of this verse to corroborate or contest the seam; it is argued from the formula shift alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading past 8:17 into the next day's date formula would merge a summary notice with the narrative it summarizes.

boundary_rationale: This part opens where the joy notice closes: web:Esth.8.17 reports “In every province and in every city, wherever the king’s commandment and his decree came, the Jews had gladness, joy, a feast and a holiday” (web:Esth.8.17), an iterative summary of the edict’s spread. Esth.9.1 instead opens with a fronted double-date superscription, וּבִשְׁנֵים֩ עָשָׂ֨ר חֹ֜דֶשׁ הוּא חֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֗ר (oshb:Esth.9.1), “Now in the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the month” (web:Esth.9.1). This verse-opening month-then-day order is not shared by the book's other appositional month-naming verses: the recurring formula '[ordinal month], that is the month [name]' — sweep: 6 book-wide (Esth.2.16, Esth.3.7, Esth.3.13, Esth.8.9, Esth.8.12, Esth.9.1) — stands verse-initial at only two of those six (Esth.3.7, Esth.9.1), and of those two, Esth.9.1 alone orders month-then-day at its own opening. Esth.3.7 instead opens month-then-YEAR, בִּשְׁנַת֙ שְׁתֵּ֣ים עֶשְׂרֵ֔ה לַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ, "in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus" (oshb:Esth.3.7), with no day element anywhere in its opening clause; Esth.8.12’s own date clause instead falls clause-medial, six words into the verse, inverting there to day-then-month, בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁ֥ה עָשָׂ֛ר לְחֹ֥דֶשׁ שְׁנֵים עָשָׂ֖ר, "on the thirteenth day of the twelfth [month]" (oshb:Esth.8.12). The book's two edict-drafting verses front no date at all: both open on the scribes-summons wayyiqtol itself, וַיִּקָּרְאוּ֩ סֹפְרֵ֨י הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ (oshb:Esth.3.12) and וַיִּקָּרְא֣וּ סֹפְרֵֽי הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ (oshb:Esth.8.9), with their own date phrases medial to the verse. Esth.9.1 then pivots on the reversal-axis clause וְנַהֲפ֣וֹךְ ה֔וּא (oshb:Esth.9.1; sweep: 1 book-wide for this exact spelling), “but it turned out that the opposite happened” (web:Esth.9.1), stated as the chapter’s own thesis before any narrative wayyiqtol resumes at web:Esth.9.2. The fear motif that closes 8:17 — “for the fear of the Jews had fallen on them” (web:Esth.8.17) — recurs at web:Esth.9.2 and web:Esth.9.3 (sweep: 3 book-wide for the fear-fell formula), a thematic bridge across the seam that does not supply 9:1’s own date-anchored superscription or its reversal clause, so the formal boundary is not erased by the shared motif.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 9:1 into the joy-notice paragraph was rejected: the fronted month-day formula and the reversal clause open a discrete legal/temporal frame that 8:17’s iterative summary does not supply.

boundary_rationale: The mainline narrative resumes with a paragraph-opening Niphal perfect — no vav-consecutive prefix — נִקְהֲל֨וּ הַיְּהוּדִ֜ים בְּעָרֵיהֶ֗ם בְּכָל מְדִינוֹת֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֳחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ לִשְׁלֹ֣חַ יָ֔ד בִּמְבַקְשֵׁ֖י רָֽעָתָ֑ם וְאִישׁ֙ לֹא עָמַ֣ד לִפְנֵיהֶ֔ם כִּֽי נָפַ֥ל פַּחְדָּ֖ם עַל כָּל הָעַמִּֽים (oshb:Esth.9.2), “the Jews gathered themselves together in their cities throughout all the provinces of the King Ahasuerus, to lay hands on those who wanted to harm them. No one could withstand them, because the fear of them had fallen on all the people” (web:Esth.9.2), reporting the engagement in general terms and its universal reception. An independent waw-fronted clause with a compound four-member subject and a participial predicate then names who helped and why: וְכָל שָׂרֵ֨י הַמְּדִינ֜וֹת וְהָאֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנִ֣ים וְהַפַּח֗וֹת וְעֹשֵׂ֤י הַמְּלָאכָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לַמֶּ֔לֶךְ מְנַשְּׂאִ֖ים אֶת הַיְּהוּדִ֑ים כִּֽי נָפַ֥ל פַּֽחַד מָרְדֳּכַ֖י עֲלֵיהֶֽם (oshb:Esth.9.3), “All the princes of the provinces, the local governors, the governors, and those who did the king's business helped the Jews, because the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them” (web:Esth.9.3) — only this verse's own final clause is causal; the clause naming the helpers is itself an independent statement, not a subordinate aside. A second, wholly causal clause follows: כִּֽי גָ֤דוֹל מָרְדֳּכַי֙ בְּבֵ֣ית הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ (oshb:Esth.9.4), “For Mordecai was great in the king’s house” (web:Esth.9.4) — a biographical aside on Mordecai’s rising fame. A single-witness mark falls one verse further in, interior to this span rather than at either of its edges: oshb:Esth.9.4 (petuchah, single-witness) is keyed to Esth.9.4 and so sits at Esth.9.4|9.5, between the biographical aside and the resumed mainline, not before either the aside or this span's own opening; disclosed here as tier-3 corroboration only, and, read in its actual direction, it would if anything weakly favor treating 9:2-9:4 apart from 9:5 rather than corroborating the grouping this row uses it for. The mainline resumes with the span's one true wayyiqtol, וַיַּכּ֤וּ הַיְּהוּדִים֙ בְּכָל אֹ֣יְבֵיהֶ֔ם מַכַּת חֶ֥רֶב וְהֶ֖רֶג וְאַבְדָ֑ן וַיַּֽעֲשׂ֥וּ בְשֹׂנְאֵיהֶ֖ם כִּרְצוֹנָֽם (oshb:Esth.9.5), “The Jews struck all their enemies with the stroke of the sword, and with slaughter and destruction, and did what they wanted to those who hated them” (web:Esth.9.5), closing the unit with a general summary of the day’s violence before the locative-fronted shift to the named citadel, וּבְשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֗ה הָרְג֤וּ הַיְּהוּדִים֙ וְאַבֵּ֔ד חֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת אִֽישׁ (oshb:Esth.9.6), that opens the next unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting off 9:3-4 as their own decision was set aside: neither carries a mainline wayyiqtol, and even though 9:3 opens as an independent clause naming the officials who helped, its own final clause and the whole of 9:4 both stay causal-explanatory to the surrounding battle report.

boundary_rationale: A locative-fronted clause opens a new, specific scene: וּבְשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֗ה הָרְג֤וּ הַיְּהוּדִים֙ וְאַבֵּ֔ד חֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת אִֽישׁ (oshb:Esth.9.6), “In the citadel of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men” (web:Esth.9.6), narrowing from the general provincial summary of web:Esth.9.5 to the named royal citadel. The register that follows, וְאֵ֧ת פַּרְשַׁנְדָּ֛תָא וְאֵ֥ת (oshb:Esth.9.7), continuing through web:Esth.9.8 and web:Esth.9.9, names Haman’s ten sons; the OSHB encoding carries ten x-paseq segs across these three verses (three at 9:7, three at 9:8, four at 9:9), each seg falling between the object marker and the following name (oshb:Esth.9.7 (paseq, single-witness), oshb:Esth.9.8 (paseq, single-witness), oshb:Esth.9.9 (paseq, single-witness)); this digital text carries no lb or milestone elements, so the traditional manuscript column layout and letter-size variants of the list are not represented here, and paseq itself is not unique to this register — it falls in twenty-seven verses book-wide (sweep: 27 book-wide). The register’s object and total are supplied by the summary verse that follows, עֲ֠שֶׂרֶת בְּנֵ֨י הָמָ֧ן בֶּֽן הַמְּדָ֛תָא צֹרֵ֥ר הַיְּהוּדִ֖ים הָרָ֑גוּ וּבַ֨בִּזָּ֔ה לֹ֥א שָׁלְח֖וּ אֶת יָדָֽם (oshb:Esth.9.10), “the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Jews’ enemy, but they didn't lay their hand on the plunder” (web:Esth.9.10) — the ten-sons phrase recurs at web:Esth.9.12, web:Esth.9.13, and web:Esth.9.14 (sweep: 4 book-wide) — closing with the plunder-refusal refrain, a refrain repeated at web:Esth.9.15 and web:Esth.9.16 (sweep: 3 book-wide), before the temporal-resumptive formula בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא בָּ֣א מִסְפַּ֧ר הַֽהֲרוּגִ֛ים בְּשׁוּשַׁ֥ן הַבִּירָ֖ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ (oshb:Esth.9.11) opens the next scene at the king’s court.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Detaching the register (9:7-9) from its summary count at 9:10 was rejected, since the list supplies names alone, with no total or object apart from the verse that follows.

boundary_rationale: A temporal-resumptive formula opens a new court scene: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא בָּ֣א מִסְפַּ֧ר הַֽהֲרוּגִ֛ים בְּשׁוּשַׁ֥ן הַבִּירָ֖ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ (oshb:Esth.9.11), “On that day, the number of those who were slain in the citadel of Susa was brought before the king” (web:Esth.9.11). This 'on that day' string recurs at two other verses book-wide, sweep: 3 book-wide (Esth.5.9, Esth.8.1, Esth.9.11): at Esth.8.1 it likewise stands verse-initial and opens a genuine court scene, but at Esth.5.9 the same string sits clause-medial, behind an exit wayyiqtol and its subject (Haman leaving the banquet); of that 3-book-wide sweep, only one of the other two members shares this verse's own opening-formula function; named that way, the device is real but narrower than a blanket 'opens court scenes' claim. A single-witness mark keyed to this verse, oshb:Esth.9.11 (setumah, single-witness), falls interior to this span, one verse in at Esth.9.11|9.12, between the count-report clause and the direct speech that follows; disclosed here as weak corroboration for that internal sub-transition, not for Esth.9.11's own status as an opener. Direct speech then carries the unit: the king's report-and-offer, וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ לְאֶסְתֵּ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֗ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֣ן (oshb:Esth.9.12), “The king said to Esther the queen … Now what is your petition? It shall be granted you” (web:Esth.9.12); Esther's reply, וַתֹּ֤אמֶר אֶסְתֵּר֙ אִם עַל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֔וֹב (oshb:Esth.9.13), “If it pleases the king” (web:Esth.9.13) — the full seventh and last member of the petition formula that recurs across the book (sweep: 7 book-wide: 1:19, 3:9, 5:4, 5:8, 7:3, 8:5, 9:13), here also naming the gallows-tree, which recurs at 8 verses book-wide, 9 tokens (sweep: 8 book-wide, 9 tokens: Esth.2.23, Esth.5.14 carrying two, Esth.6.4, Esth.7.9, Esth.7.10, Esth.8.7, Esth.9.13, Esth.9.25); and the king's decree, וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לְהֵֽעָשׂ֣וֹת כֵּ֔ן וַתִּנָּתֵ֥ן דָּ֖ת בְּשׁוּשָׁ֑ן וְאֵ֛ת עֲשֶׂ֥רֶת בְּנֵֽי הָמָ֖ן תָּלֽוּ (oshb:Esth.9.14), “The king commanded this to be done. A decree was given out in Susa” (web:Esth.9.14). The exchange closes on the execution notice; the following verse opens a new temporal marker, וַיִּֽקָּהֲל֞וּ היהודיים הַיְּהוּדִ֣ים אֲשֶׁר בְּשׁוּשָׁ֗ן גַּ֠ם בְּי֣וֹם אַרְבָּעָ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ לְחֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֔ר (oshb:Esth.9.15), “on the fourteenth day also of the month Adar” (web:Esth.9.15), for the extended killing the decree just authorized. The quoted span pairs OSHB's ketiv form with its adjacent qere at this verse, a variant noted here because the text is quoted.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at 9:13 instead of 9:14 was set aside because the exchange has no formal close until the king's command is actually carried out and the decree is issued in Susa.

boundary_rationale: A new temporal marker opens the extended killing the king’s decree authorized: וַיִּֽקָּהֲל֞וּ היהודיים הַיְּהוּדִ֣ים אֲשֶׁר בְּשׁוּשָׁ֗ן גַּ֠ם בְּי֣וֹם אַרְבָּעָ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ לְחֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֔ר (oshb:Esth.9.15), “on the fourteenth day also of the month Adar” (web:Esth.9.15); the quoted span pairs OSHB’s ketiv immediately against its qere at this verse, disclosed because the text is quoted. A contrastive subject shift then turns to the provinces, וּשְׁאָ֣ר הַיְּהוּדִ֡ים אֲשֶׁר֩ בִּמְדִינ֨וֹת הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ נִקְהֲל֣וּ וְעָמֹ֣ד עַל נַפְשָׁ֗ם וְנ֨וֹחַ֙ מֵאֹ֣יְבֵיהֶ֔ם (oshb:Esth.9.16), “The other Jews who were in the king's provinces gathered themselves together, defended their lives, had rest from their enemies” (web:Esth.9.16), reporting rest from enemies with the infinitive-spelling form that recurs at web:Esth.9.17 and web:Esth.9.18 (sweep: 3 book-wide for that spelling: 9:16, 9:17, 9:18); naming the wider root that also reaches the finite form at web:Esth.9.22 (root sweep: 4 book-wide). A summary verse then states the thirteen/fourteen pattern for the provinces, בְּיוֹם שְׁלֹשָׁ֥ה עָשָׂ֖ר לְחֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֑ר וְנ֗וֹחַ (oshb:Esth.9.17), before a second contrastive shift back to Susa’s own thirteen/fourteen/fifteen pattern, והיהודיים וְהַיְּהוּדִ֣ים אֲשֶׁר בְּשׁוּשָׁ֗ן נִקְהֲלוּ֙ בִּשְׁלֹשָׁ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ בּ֔וֹ וּבְאַרְבָּעָ֥ה עָשָׂ֖ר בּ֑וֹ וְנ֗וֹחַ בַּחֲמִשָּׁ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ בּ֔וֹ (oshb:Esth.9.18), “But the Jews who were in Susa assembled together on the thirteenth and on the fourteenth days of the month; and on the fifteenth day of that month, they rested” (web:Esth.9.18) — a quotation that likewise carries its own ketiv reading immediately beside its qere, disclosed as quoted. An 'al ken' etiological clause then opens the closing notice, naming the villagers directly: עַל כֵּ֞ן הַיְּהוּדִ֣ים הפרוזים הַפְּרָזִ֗ים (oshb:Esth.9.19), “Therefore the Jews of the villages” (web:Esth.9.19). The verse’s remainder grounds the villages’ one-day custom in the two-city pattern just narrated: הַיֹּשְׁבִים֮ בְּעָרֵ֣י הַפְּרָזוֹת֒ עֹשִׂ֗ים אֵ֠ת י֣וֹם אַרְבָּעָ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ לְחֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֔ר שִׂמְחָ֥ה וּמִשְׁתֶּ֖ה וְי֣וֹם ט֑וֹב וּמִשְׁל֥וֹחַ מָנ֖וֹת אִ֥ישׁ לְרֵעֵֽהוּ (oshb:Esth.9.19), “who live in the unwalled towns, make the fourteenth day of the month Adar a day of gladness and feasting, a holiday, and a day of sending presents of food to one another” (web:Esth.9.19), which the following mark, oshb:Esth.9.19 (petuchah, single-witness), lends weak single-witness support without driving the reading. This etiology closes the day-itself material; Mordecai’s own writing project opens the next unit at web:Esth.9.20 with a change of subject and verb of composition rather than celebration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking this span at 9:16|9:17, so the provincial notice and the day-count summary would fall in separate decisions, was set aside because 9:17 states the very pattern 9:15-16 just narrated, without any new subject or scene change.

boundary_rationale: A single-witness petuchah mark, oshb:Esth.9.19 (petuchah, single-witness), keyed to Esth.9.19 falls at this span's own opening edge — weak corroboration for the same seam this row argues from the composition-verb shift below, disclosed here and never treated as the driver. A new subject and a verb of composition open this unit: וַיִּכְתֹּ֣ב מָרְדֳּכַ֔י אֶת הַדְּבָרִ֖ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וַיִּשְׁלַ֨ח סְפָרִ֜ים (oshb:Esth.9.20), “Mordecai wrote these things, and sent letters to all the Jews” (web:Esth.9.20); the documents-plural noun sefarim, quoted above as the object of the sending verb, belongs to a small set of letter-dispatch notices across the book naming this same noun at the consonantal-skeleton tier (skeleton sweep: 6 book-wide: Esth.1.22, Esth.3.13, Esth.8.5, Esth.8.10, Esth.9.20, Esth.9.30; byte-tier sweep: 3, reaching only Esth.3.13, Esth.9.20, Esth.9.30), marking this as a fresh document inset rather than a continuation of the villages' etiology that closes the day-count material at web:Esth.9.19. Both purpose infinitives that follow stand inside a single verse: לְקַיֵּם֮ עֲלֵיהֶם֒ לִהְי֣וֹת עֹשִׂ֗ים אֵ֠ת י֣וֹם אַרְבָּעָ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ לְחֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֔ר וְאֵ֛ת יוֹם חֲמִשָּׁ֥ה עָשָׂ֖ר בּ֑וֹ בְּכָל שָׁנָ֖ה וְשָׁנָֽה (oshb:Esth.9.21), “to enjoin them that they should keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month Adar yearly” (web:Esth.9.21). The next verse opens instead on a comparative clause that grounds the observance in the day just narrated, then names the month's own reversal before a third purpose infinitive closes the inset: כַּיָּמִ֗ים אֲשֶׁר נָ֨חוּ בָהֶ֤ם הַיְּהוּדִים֙ מֵא֣וֹיְבֵיהֶ֔ם וְהַחֹ֗דֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר֩ נֶהְפַּ֨ךְ לָהֶ֤ם מִיָּגוֹן֙ לְשִׂמְחָ֔ה וּמֵאֵ֖בֶל לְי֣וֹם ט֑וֹב לַעֲשׂ֣וֹת אוֹתָ֗ם יְמֵי֙ מִשְׁתֶּ֣ה וְשִׂמְחָ֔ה וּמִשְׁל֤וֹחַ מָנוֹת֙ אִ֣ישׁ לְרֵעֵ֔הוּ וּמַתָּנ֖וֹת לָֽאֶבְיוֹנִֽים (oshb:Esth.9.22), “as the days in which the Jews had rest from their enemies, and the month which was turned to them from sorrow to gladness, and from mourning into a holiday; that they should make them days of feasting and gladness, and of sending presents of food to one another, and gifts to the needy” (web:Esth.9.22). The reversal-nifal clause at the verse's center, וְהַחֹ֗דֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר֩ נֶהְפַּ֨ךְ לָהֶ֤ם מִיָּגוֹן֙ לְשִׂמְחָ֔ה וּמֵאֵ֖בֶל לְי֣וֹם ט֑וֹב (oshb:Esth.9.22), carries a spelling distinct from 9:1's own thesis clause: sweep: 1 book-wide for this exact nifal form, counted separately from the nifal reversal clause at 9:1; both forms are nifal, with no stem contrast between them. This inset stays with its own frame through the instruction it issues; וְקִבֵּל֙ הַיְּהוּדִ֔ים אֵ֥ת אֲשֶׁר הֵחֵ֖לּוּ לַעֲשׂ֑וֹת וְאֵ֛ת אֲשֶׁר כָּתַ֥ב מָרְדֳּכַ֖י אֲלֵיהֶֽם (oshb:Esth.9.23), a change of grammatical subject and verb that opens the confirmation material rather than continuing Mordecai’s own instruction.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this unit through 9:23 to include the Jews' acceptance was set aside, since 9:23 changes both the grammatical subject and the verb from writing to receiving.

boundary_rationale: The subject and verb change from Mordecai’s writing to the Jews’ reception: וְקִבֵּל֙ הַיְּהוּדִ֔ים אֵ֥ת אֲשֶׁר הֵחֵ֖לּוּ לַעֲשׂ֑וֹת וְאֵ֛ת אֲשֶׁר כָּתַ֥ב מָרְדֳּכַ֖י אֲלֵיהֶֽם (oshb:Esth.9.23), “The Jews accepted the custom that they had begun, as Mordecai had written to them” (web:Esth.9.23), opening the confirmation material rather than continuing the letter’s own instructions at web:Esth.9.22. A backgrounded causal clause then recounts Haman’s plot in full, כִּי֩ הָמָ֨ן בֶּֽן הַמְּדָ֜תָא הָֽאֲגָגִ֗י צֹרֵר֙ כָּל הַיְּהוּדִ֔ים חָשַׁ֥ב עַל הַיְּהוּדִ֖ים לְאַבְּדָ֑ם וְהִפִּ֥יל פּוּר֙ ה֣וּא הַגּוֹרָ֔ל לְהֻמָּ֖ם וּֽלְאַבְּדָֽם (oshb:Esth.9.24), “because Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast “Pur”, that is the lot, to consume them and to destroy them” (web:Esth.9.24) — naming the pur-casting formula that also recurs at web:Esth.3.7 (sweep: 2 book-wide) — and the gallows-tree that closes the flashback at web:Esth.9.25. A qatal 'al ken' clause then opens the naming of the festival; no wayyiqtol falls anywhere in this span (checked verse-by-verse against 9:21-9:28's own bytes: every vav-initial form there is conjunctive-waw plus qatal or participle rather than the wayyiqtol shape), and the narrative mainline does not resume until Esther's own writing at web:Esth.9.29: עַל כֵּ֡ן קָֽרְאוּ֩ לַיָּמִ֨ים הָאֵ֤לֶּה פוּרִים֙ עַל שֵׁ֣ם הַפּ֔וּר (oshb:Esth.9.26), “Therefore they called these days “Purim”, from the word “Pur.”” (web:Esth.9.26). The plene spelling recurs at web:Esth.9.28 and web:Esth.9.29 (sweep: 3 book-wide: 9:26, 9:28, 9:29); the articled defective spelling at 9:31-9:32 is not reached by a contiguous skeleton sweep of the plene spelling, though the two share every consonant but the article prefix (sweep: 2 book-wide for the articled form, Esth.9.31 and Esth.9.32; the bare defective spelling without the article is itself a substring of sefarim and sweeps 8, the same six verses the neighboring letter-dispatch count reaches plus 9:31 and 9:32); WEB renders both spellings as the single term 'Purim' a reader sees (term sweep: 5 book-wide). A ratification formula then closes the block, קִיְּמ֣וּ וקבל וְקִבְּל֣וּ הַיְּהוּדִים֩ עֲלֵיהֶ֨ם (oshb:Esth.9.27), a quotation that carries OSHB’s ketiv reading immediately beside its qere for this verse, disclosed as quoted, and a remembrance clause, וְהַיָּמִ֣ים הָ֠אֵלֶּה נִזְכָּרִ֨ים וְנַעֲשִׂ֜ים בְּכָל דּ֣וֹר וָד֗וֹר (oshb:Esth.9.28), “these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation” (web:Esth.9.28), where weak single-witness corroboration follows in the mark oshb:Esth.9.28 (setumah, single-witness). Esther’s own composition then opens the next document inset at web:Esth.9.29 with a new subject, verb of writing, and explicit self-designation as 'this second letter.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the Haman flashback (9:24-25) into its own decision was rejected, because the 'al ken' clause that opens 9:26 continues, in the same qatal register, what the causal clause of 9:24 sets up, so the two verses function as one causal-resultative unit rather than two independent scenes.

boundary_rationale: A new subject and verb of composition open this unit, now with Esther named first: וַ֠תִּכְתֹּב אֶסְתֵּ֨ר הַמַּלְכָּ֧ה בַת אֲבִיחַ֛יִל וּמָרְדֳּכַ֥י הַיְּהוּדִ֖י אֶת כָּל תֹּ֑קֶף לְקַיֵּ֗ם אֵ֣ת אִגֶּ֧רֶת הַפּוּרִ֛ים הַזֹּ֖את הַשֵּׁנִֽית (oshb:Esth.9.29), “Then Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote with all authority to confirm this second letter of Purim” (web:Esth.9.29) — the verse's own final word, הַשֵּׁנִֽית, 'the second' (oshb:Esth.9.29), is the explicit self-designation that marks this as a distinct document from the confirmation material closing at web:Esth.9.28. The setumah keyed to Esth.9.28, oshb:Esth.9.28 (setumah, single-witness), sits at this unit's own front edge as well — the same single-witness mark the neighboring confirmation block discloses at its own rear edge — offering tier-3 corroboration on both sides of the seam without settling it. The letter-dispatch noun recurs, וַיִּשְׁלַ֨ח סְפָרִ֜ים אֶל כָּל הַיְּהוּדִ֗ים אֶל שֶׁ֨בַע וְעֶשְׂרִ֤ים וּמֵאָה֙ מְדִינָ֔ה מַלְכ֖וּת אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ דִּבְרֵ֥י שָׁל֖וֹם וֶאֱמֶֽת (oshb:Esth.9.30), “He sent letters to all the Jews in the hundred twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus with words of peace and truth” (web:Esth.9.30); the hundred-twenty-seven-province numeral, אֶל שֶׁ֨בַע וְעֶשְׂרִ֤ים וּמֵאָה֙ מְדִינָ֔ה (oshb:Esth.9.30) — its three numeral words alone echo the same formula opening the book and naming the counter-edict above the byte tier (accent_stripped and skeleton sweep: 3 book-wide: 1:1, 8:9, 9:30; the full quoted phrase including 'province' is unique to this verse at every tier, byte sweep: 1 book-wide) — an empire-wide-scope echo spanning the whole book. A purpose clause follows (web:Esth.9.31), closing with a fasting notice, דִּבְרֵ֥י הַצֹּמ֖וֹת וְזַעֲקָתָֽם (oshb:Esth.9.31), “in the matter of the fastings and their mourning” (web:Esth.9.31) — the definite plural of the same fasting noun attested at 4:3 (sweep: 2 book-wide for that noun: 4:3, and 9:31 in its defective plural); the finite verb forms of that root stand only at 4:16 (sweep: 1 book-wide, two tokens: an imperative and a first-person yiqtol) — 4:3 itself carries the noun inside a coordinated mourning series, not a finite form. A closing ratification notice ends the unit and the whole institution sequence, וּמַאֲמַ֣ר אֶסְתֵּ֔ר קִיַּ֕ם דִּבְרֵ֥י הַפֻּרִ֖ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וְנִכְתָּ֖ב בַּסֵּֽפֶר (oshb:Esth.9.32), “The commandment of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim; and it was written in the book” (web:Esth.9.32), where a single-witness mark follows, oshb:Esth.9.32 (petuchah, single-witness), offering weak corroboration at the level Writings marks allow. A new subject and topic then open the epilogue at web:Esth.10.1, turning from Purim to royal tribute.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 9:29 as a continuation of the confirmation block instead of a new document was set aside, because the verse explicitly labels itself a second, distinct letter rather than an extension of the first.

boundary_rationale: A new subject and topic open this final unit: וַיָּשֶׂם֩ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ אחשרש אֲחַשְׁוֵר֧וֹשׁ מַ֛ס עַל הָאָ֖רֶץ וְאִיֵּ֥י הַיָּֽם (oshb:Esth.10.1), a quotation that carries OSHB’s ketiv reading immediately beside its qere for the king’s name in this verse, disclosed as quoted, “King Ahasuerus laid a tribute on the land and on the islands of the sea” (web:Esth.10.1), turning from the Purim institution that closes at web:Esth.9.32 to a royal-administration notice naming the king in full title. Immediately before this span begins, Esth.9.32 carries its own petuchah, oshb:Esth.9.32 (petuchah, single-witness); named here as front-edge corroboration, tier-3 and non-driving. The chronicle-citation formula follows, וְכָל מַעֲשֵׂ֤ה תָקְפּוֹ֙ וּגְב֣וּרָת֔וֹ וּפָרָשַׁת֙ גְּדֻלַּ֣ת מָרְדֳּכַ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר גִּדְּל֖וֹ הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ הֲלוֹא הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל סֵ֨פֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י הַיָּמִ֔ים לְמַלְכֵ֖י מָדַ֥י וּפָרָֽס (oshb:Esth.10.2), “Aren't all the acts of his power and of his might, and the full account of the greatness of Mordecai, to which the king advanced him, written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia” (web:Esth.10.2). The closing clause of that formula, עַל סֵ֨פֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י הַיָּמִ֔ים לְמַלְכֵ֖י מָדַ֥י וּפָרָֽס (oshb:Esth.10.2), is unique to this verse at every tier — byte sweep: 1 book-wide, skeleton sweep: 1 book-wide — since it opens with the separate-word preposition al; the exposition's Bigthan-and-Teresh notice instead closes on a prefixed-bet form of the shorter core phrase, sefer divrei hayamim, matching this verse's own core phrase already at the accent_stripped tier (accent_stripped sweep: 2 book-wide: Esth.2.23, Esth.10.2; at byte tier each verse's pointed form is unique to itself, sweep: 1 book-wide for each, since the two verses' cantillation accents differ even though the underlying consonants and vowel points agree). A closing tribute to Mordecai ends the book, כִּ֣י מָרְדֳּכַ֣י הַיְּהוּדִ֗י מִשְׁנֶה֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ וְגָדוֹל֙ לַיְּהוּדִ֔ים וְרָצ֖וּי לְרֹ֣ב אֶחָ֑יו דֹּרֵ֥שׁ טוֹב֙ לְעַמּ֔וֹ וְדֹבֵ֥ר שָׁל֖וֹם לְכָל זַרְעֽוֹ (oshb:Esth.10.3), “For Mordecai the Jew was next to King Ahasuerus, and great among the Jews … seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his descendants” (web:Esth.10.3), a benediction-style summary that supplies its own closing rather than opening onto further narration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this epilogue into Esther's second letter as one continuous closing unit was set aside, since 10:1 changes both subject and topic entirely, from Purim's ratification to an unrelated tribute notice.
